mSv.simple: A measurement of radiation absorbed by the human body.
mSv.detail: On Earth, you receive about 3 mSv per year from natural rocks and sunlight. In deep space, cosmic rays and solar flares can deliver hundreds of mSv, so astronauts need thick shields!
mSv.citation: NASA Space Radiation Program Element / NCRP Report No. 153

Sol.simple: One day and night on planet Mars.
Sol.detail: A Martian Sol lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35 seconds. That is just about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day!
Sol.citation: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Mars Exploration

LunarDay.simple: The Moon takes about 28 Earth days to spin once.
LunarDay.detail: That means 14 straight Earth days of blistering sunlight, followed by 14 Earth days of freezing dark! At the South Pole rim, high crater peaks get sunlight almost 86% of the year.
LunarDay.citation: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA Team

Regolith.simple: The crushed rock, dust, and mineral soil covering the Moon and Mars.
Regolith.detail: Space dirt is very sharp and dusty, but piled into thick sandbags over a habitat dome, it makes an amazing natural shield against radiation and micrometeorites!
Regolith.citation: NASA Artemis Base Camp Surface Concepts

Kilowatt.simple: A unit measuring how much electric power a base uses.
Kilowatt.detail: 1 kilowatt is 1,000 watts — enough to run a microwave oven. A full Artemis base needs 20 to 40 kilowatts to heat rooms, make oxygen, and charge rovers.

ECLSS.simple: The Environmental Control and Life Support System.
ECLSS.detail: The machine that scrubs carbon dioxide from breathing air, produces fresh oxygen from water, and recycles 98% of crew moisture and sweat into crystal-clean drinking water!
ECLSS.citation: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center ECLSS Development

CME.simple: A giant cannon blast of magnetic solar gas shot out from the Sun.
CME.detail: When the Sun has a storm, it can fling billions of tons of super-heated plasma into space at millions of miles per hour. If it hits an outpost, radiation levels soar!
CME.citation: NASA Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, and Information (DONKI)

SPE.simple: A storm of fast, high-energy protons hurled by the Sun.
SPE.detail: These tiny energetic particles travel at almost the speed of light. Without magnetic deflection or deep storm shelters, they can damage human DNA and computer chips.
SPE.citation: NASA Heliophysics Division / DONKI Space Weather Service

EVA.simple: Extravehicular Activity: when an astronaut steps outside in a spacesuit.
EVA.detail: Spacewalks are vital for repairs and collecting ice, but astronauts must carry their own oxygen tank and are exposed to space radiation outside the habitat walls.
EVA.citation: NASA Johnson Space Center EVA Office

MOXIE.simple: Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment.
MOXIE.detail: A real gold box aboard NASA's Perseverance rover that takes thin Martian carbon dioxide gas (CO2) and cracks it into breathable oxygen (O2) like a mechanical tree!
MOXIE.citation: NASA Perseverance Rover MOXIE Team / MIT Haystack Observatory

Kilopower.simple: A safe, compact nuclear fission power source for space bases.
Kilopower.detail: Unlike solar panels that stop when night falls or dust storms brew, Kilopower provides a steady, reliable 10 to 40 kilowatts 24/7 for over 10 years.

moon.name: Artemis Base Camp
moon.tagline: Peak of Eternal Light — Extreme temperatures, ancient polar water ice.

data_citations.fact: Mapped Shackleton Crater rim elevation and identified Peaks of Eternal Light with 86% annual sunlight.
Recorded coldest temperatures in the solar system (-246°C / 27 Kelvin) inside permanently shadowed craters where water ice survives for billions of years.

data_citations.instrument: Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER)
data_citations.fact: Measured deep space Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) delivering 0.35 to 0.45 mSv/day at the lunar surface.

mars.name: Jezero Outpost Alpha
mars.tagline: Ancient Riverbed — Dynamic dust devils, CO2 atmosphere, frozen subsurface aquifers.

data_citations.fact: Provides daily records of Martian air temperature (-85°C to -10°C), atmospheric pressure (610 Pa), and optical dust thickness (tau).
Proven technology producing 6 to 12 grams of breathable oxygen per hour from the 95% CO2 Martian atmosphere.

data_citations.instrument: Mars Science Laboratory Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD)
data_citations.fact: Confirmed surface radiation dose rate of ~0.64 mSv/day during solar minimum, proving deep shelters are required for long stays.

studies.title: GeneLab: Cellular Stress & DNA Double-Strand Breaks Under High-LET Space Radiation
studies.clinical_note: Identified repair pathways activated when astronauts receive >20 mSv, establishing the early caution zone.

studies.title: GeneLab: Musculoskeletal Degradation & Bone Mineral Density Loss in Partial Gravity
studies.clinical_note: Documented 1.2% bone density loss per 30 days without daily 2-hour resistive exercise and balanced hydration.

studies.title: NASA Space Flight Human-System Standard: Radiation Health
studies.clinical_note: Limits cumulative career exposure to keep risk of exposure-induced death (REID) below 3% at 95% confidence interval.

donki_weather_catalog.intensity: X4.5 Solar Flare + Fast Halo CME (1,450 km/s)
donki_weather_catalog.sensor: GOES-16 Solar Ultraviolet Imager & SOHO LASCO C3
donki_weather_catalog.description: Massive coronal mass ejection directed toward the inner solar system. High-energy protons arriving within hours.

donki_weather_catalog.sensor: STEREO-A Ahead Plastic Sensor & ACE EPAM
donki_weather_catalog.description: Coronal shock front producing intense flux of protons >100 MeV. Moderate radiation spike expected.

donki_weather_catalog.intensity: Nominal Deep Galactic Cosmic Ray Stream
donki_weather_catalog.description: Steady background galactic cosmic rays originating outside our solar system.

tactical_events.title: ALERT: X-Class Solar Particle Storm Inbound!
tactical_events.science_note: Real NASA DONKI records show an X4.5 coronal mass ejection can send billions of tons of high-energy protons directly across planetary surfaces.
tactical_events.dialogue: Flight Director: 'Commander, satellites detect a massive solar flare! Fast proton shockwave arriving in 45 minutes. How do we configure the base?'

choices.label: Option A: 80% Power to Active Magnetic Deflectors & Regolith Bunkers
choices.preview: Safe Crew Dose (+3 mSv) | Life Support drops to Emergency Power | Science paused
choices.feedback: Engineering Report: The active magnetic coil deflected 92% of energetic protons into space. The crew remained safe inside the regolith vault. ECLSS was strained on backup battery, but no permanent injury occurred.

choices.label: Option B: Power Science Scanners to Harvest Rare Coronal Data
choices.preview: Massive Science Yield (+140 Pts) | Heavy Radiation Dose (+38 mSv) | Medical Alert
choices.feedback: Science Report: Unprecedented solar particle observations captured! But crew radiation monitors flashed amber-red (OSDR threshold alert). Crew shows early signs of radiation fatigue and requires medical downtime.

tactical_events.title: ENVIRONMENTAL HAZARD: Solar Blackout Approaching!
tactical_events.science_note: Martian dust storms (or the 14-day Lunar polar night) can drop sunlight by over 75%, plunging temperatures to -120°C and starving solar arrays of power.
tactical_events.dialogue: Base Engineer: 'Commander, dust optical depth is climbing to tau 3.8 (or lunar shadow is advancing). Our solar panels will drop from 30 kW down to 4 kW! What is our energy doctrine?'

choices.label: Option 1: Shut Down MOXIE / Scrubbers & Switch to Pressurized Tanks
choices.preview: Conserves 14 kW Power | Burns 120 L Water/O2 Reserves | Science slows
choices.feedback: Resource Log: By throttling power-hungry air scrubbers and thermal pumps, our Kilopower generator carried the habitat through the storm without draining the battery bank. We dipped into stored reserves as planned.

choices.label: Option 2: Fire Auxiliary Fuel Cells to Maintain Full Habitat Power
choices.preview: Full Science & Life Support maintained | Consumes 220 L Stored Reserves & Battery Wear
choices.feedback: Engineering Log: The base ran at 100% capacity and science continued uninterrupted! However, our backup fuel cells burned through 180 liters of precious reserves. One more storm like this will leave us bone dry.

tactical_events.title: EXPLORATION TARGET: Subsurface Water Ice Anomaly Discovered!
tactical_events.science_note: Orbital radar detected a rich pocket of pure water ice 1.5 meters under the regolith. Ice can be melted for drinking, split into breathing oxygen, or converted into rocket propellant!
tactical_events.dialogue: Astrobiologist: 'We located a rich cryo-ice deposit 2 kilometers outside the perimeter. How should we extract the core samples?'

choices.label: Option A: 2-Person Spacewalk (EVA) with Thermal Core Drill
choices.preview: Yields +350 L Water Ice & High Quality Science (+110 Pts) | Crew Fatigue & Suit O2 Consumed
choices.feedback: Mission Log: Astronauts completed a flawless 6-hour EVA! They harvested 350 liters of pristine water ice and gathered pristine core stratigraphy. The crew is tired and slightly radiated, but our water reserves are replenished!

choices.label: Option B: Deploy Autonomous Rover Drill
choices.preview: Zero Crew Risk (0 mSv) | High Power Draw (-22% Battery) | Slower Extraction (+120 L Water)
choices.feedback: Robotics Log: Rover drill navigated automatically through the boulders and drilled 3 test cores. Extraction was slow and battery-intensive, but the crew rested comfortably inside the habitat with zero radiation exposure.

tactical_events.title: SYSTEM FAILURE: Sabatier Water Condenser Seal Ruptured!
tactical_events.science_note: Life support water recovery loops operate under high pressure and temperature. On the ISS, urine and humidity recyclers require constant preventative upkeep to maintain a 98% water recovery rate.
tactical_events.dialogue: Systems Engineer: 'Pressure sensors in the ECLSS Sabatier loop are sounding! We are venting 15 liters of recycled water per hour into the exhaust separator.'

choices.label: Option 1: Emergency Manual Overhaul (Divert Base Power to Diagnostics)
choices.preview: Permanent Fix (+15% ECLSS Reliability) | Base Enters Low-Power Standby | Wear on Tools
choices.feedback: Engineering Log: The crew disassembled the condenser and replaced the Teflon gasket using 3D-printed spare seals. The leak is 100% sealed, restoring full recycling efficiency!

choices.label: Option 2: Apply Quick Polymer Patch & Implement Strict Water Rationing
choices.preview: Conserves Power (+10% Battery) | Crew Water Rationing (-12% Health) | Risk of Re-leak
choices.feedback: Medical Report: Quick sealant slowed the leak, but strict 1.5L/day water rationing has caused mild crew dehydration and headache fatigue (OSDR health impact). Water is leaking at a slow trickle.

tactical_events.title: OPPORTUNITY: Deep Space Network High-Bandwidth Alignment!
tactical_events.science_note: NASA's Deep Space Network dishes in Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra provide high-bandwidth Ka-band optical communication links back to Earth Mission Control.
tactical_events.dialogue: Flight Director: 'Commander, Earth alignment gives us a 4-hour ultra-high bandwidth link. We can upload our high-resolution scientific survey data or calibrate planetary navigation.'

choices.label: Option A: Crank Ka-Band Transmitters to Stream Terabytes of Raw Science
choices.preview: Massive Science Score (+160 Pts) | High Transmitter Power Draw (-16% Battery)
choices.feedback: Mission Control: 'Earth scientists have received the complete spectroscopy dataset! Congratulations Commander, this is Nobel-worthy planetary research!'

choices.label: Option B: Send Compressed Summary Only & Keep Batteries Fully Charged
choices.preview: Moderate Science (+40 Pts) | 100% Battery Reserves Maintained for Safety
choices.feedback: Operations Log: Standard telemetry packet verified by Madrid ground station. High battery reserve preserved for unknown environmental anomalies ahead.
